workshops.title: SwiftUI workbench: edit one draft from two places
workshops.summary: Build the scratch iOS app, then follow an edit through its owner and bindings. Try navigation, presentations, previews, and a local task that accepts only the current input.

simple.story: A family writes a shopping list on one whiteboard. Someone reads it from the kitchen; someone else walks over from the dining table to edit it. There is still only one list. When Milk changes to Oats, both readers see Oats. Copying the board into two separate notebooks would create another problem: someone would have to keep the copies in step. The useful arrangement is one owned list and several ways to read or change it. Erasing the board ends that in-memory list unless someone saved it elsewhere.
simple.meaning: The app-owned PracticeDraft is one shared model. Gallery and its sheet read that same reference, and bindings let controls write into it. SwiftUI views describe how to display current values; they are not durable screen objects or a storage system.

example.before: PracticeDraft has priority 1. The proposed priority editor appears in Gallery and in the sheet, and both use the same draft.
example.change: Change the sheet's priority Stepper from 1 to 2, then dismiss the sheet.
example.after: Gallery reads priority 2 from the same draft. A task input containing card Alpha and priority 2 replaces Alpha/1; only the current combination may set the final label.

picture.caption: A sheet edit writes into one owned draft and Gallery reads the new value.

items.label: Sheet control
items.text: A binding reads and writes the draft's priority.

items.label: One change
items.text: The Stepper changes priority from 1 to 2.

items.text: Its view description reads 2 from the same model.

words.meaning: A description of interface content derived from current inputs.
Read and write access to a value owned elsewhere.
Tracking the model properties a view reads so changes can update its description.
Values and model references supplied through a SwiftUI view tree.
The selected simulator or device environment where an app will run.
View-associated asynchronous work that restarts when its declared input changes.

simple.remember: Keep one owner for an editable value and give editors access to that value.
simple.boundary: The whiteboard explains one source of truth, not SwiftUI view lifetime. Views can be recreated as descriptions, while @State ownership follows identity. Observation does not save the draft. Task cancellation is cooperative, and a successful build does not establish a launched screen or device interaction.

sections.title: Build an app, then check that it launches
sections.html:
An app target is the product Xcode builds into an application. A scheme selects build and launch actions; a destination selects the simulator or device environment. SwiftUI descriptions need all three before you can see a screen. Compose gives you a useful starting point for describing UI, while this project supplies the iOS app boundary. Open SwiftUIWorkbench, choose its shared scheme, and select an installed iPhone Simulator. It has no package dependencies, company SDKs, team identifier, credentials, or remote fixture service. Both the app and widget require iOS 17. The project selects Swift 5 language mode, even if the installed compiler is newer. Compiler release, language mode, deployment floor, and simulator runtime are separate facts.

Read the lab README before running. The first checkpoint is a successful generic simulator build using its exact command and a temporary DerivedData directory. The second is an installed, launched application showing Gallery, UIKit, Stores, and Platform tabs. Keep these checkpoints separate: compiling both architectures does not establish that the process launched, that a permission prompt appeared, or that a widget refreshed. In the authoring environment, simulator services were unavailable; the README records compilation evidence and leaves interactive evidence pending.

The application entry point uses @main and conforms to App. A WindowGroup describes its window content. App-owned services construct a SwiftData container and a programmatic Core Data stack, but do not request runtime permissions or contact a provider. If the SwiftData container fails to open, a visible error replaces the main interface. That is preferable to deleting a store or crashing to make a tutorial appear successful. Work through sessions 071 and 074 for tools and previews, then reconnect this target with the ownership discussion in sessions 009 and 034.

sections.title: Follow an edit back to its owner
sections.html:
A state owner keeps the value that editors share. Here PracticeDraft is a reference type: passing it to another view can refer to the same object. @Observable tracks property reads for updates. @MainActor isolates access under the main-actor contract; it does not create a separate thread or save data. The app holds its service owner in @State, and that owner retains the draft. Gallery and its sheet receive the same draft through the environment. This resembles sharing a Compose state holder through a tree, while SwiftUI has its own identity and tracking rules. The controls below use a binding to edit that existing draft.

struct DraftEditor: View {
    @Bindable var draft: PracticeDraft
    var body: some View {
        TextField("Synthetic name", text: $draft.name)
        Toggle("Enable demo reminder", isOn: $draft.reminders)
    }
}

@Bindable creates projections such as $draft.name; it does not create a second draft. The text: argument requires a binding because typing writes back. A read-only summary receives an ordinary reference and reads its computed validity. Its body becomes dependent on the properties those computations read. In Kotlin you often pass a value plus an event lambda; a SwiftUI binding packages corresponding read and write access. Domain validation still belongs to your application.

Checkpoint: type a name, open the editor sheet, change it there, and dismiss. The gallery summary should reflect the same value. Change the task picker or move between tabs; these unrelated changes should not reset the app-owned draft. Force-quit and relaunch separately: this draft is in memory and has no restoration contract. The reminder toggle only demonstrates data flow. Actual scheduling requires the explicit Platform button. Sessions 075, 076, and 078 turn these distinctions into ownership decisions; sessions 009 and 013 explain why duplicating editable state across parent and child creates synchronization problems.

sections.title: Put controls together and supply preview values
sections.html:
A control displays a value and offers an action, such as typing text or choosing a number. The Form contains TextField, Toggle, Stepper, Slider, Picker, DatePicker, TextEditor, and buttons. Each expects an appropriate value type: a slider binds to a floating-point value, and a picker selection must match its tags. Accessibility labels give compact controls useful spoken names. @FocusState stores which editor has focus; Done clears it explicitly. A keyboard type suggests an input method, and a content type tells the system what the field means. Neither validates the entered text. This scratch form uses synthetic values rather than contact details or real account information.

WorkshopCard conforms to ViewModifier. Its body receives the content and returns a padded background description. The workshopCard() extension makes the policy reusable without globally changing every view. WorkshopButtonStyle instead receives a button configuration, reads pressed state and the environment's enabled value, and describes the button's appearance. Its tap behavior remains in the Button action. These are distinct extension points, not equivalent names for a theme. Modifier order changes which bounds receive padding or a background; inspect the implementation before moving calls.

The custom workbenchPolicy environment key distributes a label and tint. The Observation environment distributes actual model references. Neither supplies automatic lifecycle management. The preview entry point injects all required references and uses memory-only containers, so a preview does not edit the persistent scratch stores. The accessibility preview raises Dynamic Type to exercise layout. Named previews are source fixtures, not proof that Canvas rendered successfully. Missing environment injection can fail at runtime even when a view's declaration compiles.

Checkpoint: change only the preview policy to teal and a distinct fixture label; confirm the preview differs from the application's normal policy without changing shared global state. Then inspect controls with an empty name and a long name. Sessions 072–074 cover view syntax and fixture construction, 078 covers dependency distribution, and 031 explains modifier and layout contracts. The SF Symbols in this project are system assets; the lab does not teach an asset-catalog export pipeline.

sections.title: Own routes and presentations separately
sections.html:
A route is a value saying which content to show next. The router stores an array of GalleryRoute values. Each enum case names a fixture card or the split gallery. NavigationStack(path:) binds to that route array; navigationDestination(for:) maps each route value to a view description. An item route carries a stable fixture identifier. It does not carry a live database object. This lets a validated link or local notification choose a known fixture without moving a context-bound persistence record into navigation. Session 079 builds this mechanism, and session 010 compares UIKit coordinators. Stack ownership still needs an explicit choice; every screen does not automatically need its own stack.

The app's TabView selection belongs to the same router. A validated incoming route can select Gallery and replace its path. The split gallery uses NavigationSplitView with optional selection and an independent detail column. Wide windows can show both columns; compact environments adapt them. This demonstration is deliberately small: it does not encode process restoration, multi-window routing, universal links, or authentication gates. Those are explicit further tasks, not properties supplied by naming a view NavigationStack.

A sheet uses an optional identifiable choice; a full-screen cover uses a Boolean. The distinction shows two common presentation contracts. The cover reads dismiss from its own environment so it dismisses its presentation. Sheet editing receives the existing draft. The popover may adapt on compact devices. An alert displays validation feedback, while a confirmation dialog asks before clearing the name. None of these actions inserts a record or requests a system permission.

Checkpoint: push Alpha, return, open the split gallery, and select Beta. Open and dismiss each presentation using its intended control, then cancel the reset confirmation. The draft should survive cancellation. Test both iPhone and iPad destinations before claiming adaptive navigation works. Sessions 080 and 034 explain presentation and scene boundaries; 035 combines identity, editing, and terminal outcomes into a feature review.

sections.title: Accept a task result only while its input is current
sections.html:
An asynchronous task can pause before producing an answer. The gallery uses task(id:) to delay a synthetic result. SwiftUI associates the task with view identity and restarts it when the declared input changes. The task captures the selected identifier, awaits a short sleep, checks cancellation, and compares that identifier with the current selection before assigning its label. Cancellation requests stopping; the task must cooperate. A Task handle or an async declaration does not by itself reject an old result. The final comparison makes this example's acceptance rule visible. SwiftUI's body describes the screen; it should not start a fresh request every time the body is evaluated.

Pull to refresh also performs a local cancellable delay before replacing fixtures. There is no URLSession call behind the gesture. onChange increments a name-edit counter to demonstrate observation, but it does not copy the name into another source of truth. These mechanisms answer different questions: a task owns asynchronous work; a change handler reacts to a value transition; state owns the displayed value. Body evaluation should remain an interface description, not an instruction to start a request repeatedly.

Checkpoint: switch the task picker from Alpha to Beta before the delay finishes. The final label must identify Beta. Leave Gallery during a delay, return, and record what the current task shows. Use session 081 alongside session 011 for suspension and lifetime, and session 084 for a handoff that names executed checks. This is a practice observation to perform, not an author-supplied claim that every race has been reproduced. Deterministic concurrency gates belong to the separate host lab; this UI delay makes the mechanism visible but does not replace controlled ordering tests.

Keep a short evidence ledger: compiler version, destination, command exit, launched screen, observed input sequence, resulting label, and remaining uncertainty. Do not mark a learner exercise complete merely because the companion already contains examples. Your exercise adds a new behavior below, and your own acceptance record establishes what you actually practiced.

exercise.brief: Add priority 1...3 to the shared draft. Edit it in Gallery and its sheet, then include priority in the local task's input so old combinations cannot replace the current result.
steps: Build the unchanged target, then install and launch it when a simulator is available. Record compilation and launch as separate results.
Add priority to PracticeDraft, starting at 1. Make a child editor that receives only Binding<Int> and limits the value to 1...3.
Use that editor in the shared DraftEditor and read draft.priority directly in the summary.
Make the task input contain both card ID and priority. Changing either value must restart work and retire the old combination.
Change priority while a task is pending, including from the sheet. Record both editors' values and the final task label; keep course progress separate.
acceptance: Both editors change one app-owned value rather than synchronizing two copies.
A current task result contains the selected card and priority; obsolete work never overwrites it.
Preview fixtures supply the required model and policy.
The handoff separates app compilation, actual simulator interaction, and pending device checks.
exercise.solution:
Add var priority = 1 to the observable draft. Define PriorityEditor with @Binding var priority: Int and give its Stepper $priority with range 1...3. DraftEditor passes $draft.priority, so Gallery and the sheet edit one value. Moving the sheet's Stepper to 2 must make the Gallery summary read 2. The summary reads draft.priority directly; it needs no second stored priority and no notification to keep a copy synchronized.

struct TaskInput: Equatable {
    let card: String
    let priority: Int
}

// In the gallery, derive this from the two current values.
// Attach .task(id: input) to the existing view.
let captured = input
try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(700))
try Task.checkCancellation()
guard captured == TaskInput(card: selectedTask, priority: draft.priority) else { return }
taskStatus = "Current: \(captured.card), priority \(captured.priority)"

The snippet shows the successful path inside the task's existing do/catch; it is target-dependent SwiftUI code, not a standalone program. A computed input avoids storing a third synchronized copy. Here selectedTask reads the current State source and draft.priority reads the retained model at the commit boundary. Do not compare captured with the same immutable local input captured by the closure: that comparison is always equal and establishes no freshness. Input equality and cancellation serve this UI example; an independently restarted operation or account switch also needs the request generation/epoch contract taught in the host gates. Change the priority while the delay is pending and confirm the old combination does not win. Observation triggers reevaluation because the computed input reads the draft property. If the actor cannot suspend between the final guard and assignment, another main-actor mutation cannot interleave inside that commit.

For the ownership explanation, draw the app retaining services, services retaining the draft, and two editors borrowing bindings. Record that app termination discards this model. A successful xcodebuild establishes compiler and packaging evidence; a screenshot or interaction log from a launched destination establishes the separate visual checkpoint. The supplied source is a worked companion, and this extension remains learner work until you implement and verify it yourself.

quiz.question: What gives the sheet and gallery one editable draft?
options: Their identical TextField titles
An app-retained observable model with bindings into that reference
Adding onChange handlers that copy every property
quiz.explanation: Ownership keeps one reference alive; bindings edit its properties. Observation tracks reads but does not create persistence or synchronize independent models.

quiz.question: What does a successful generic simulator build establish?
options: The app and extension compiled and packaged for that SDK
VoiceOver navigation passed
The device accepted notification permission
quiz.explanation: Compilation and packaging are executed build evidence. Launch, assistive technology, permissions, and hardware behavior require separate runtime checks.

quiz.question: Why check cancellation and the captured task input before updating the label?
options: Task.sleep always returns on a background thread
It automatically persists the label
An obsolete task must not commit after its input is replaced
quiz.explanation: Cancellation is cooperative and a completed operation can belong to an obsolete input. The commit guard makes that ownership explicit.

workshops.title: Usable UI: keep text readable and actions reachable
workshops.summary: Try large text, spoken controls, stable UIKit row IDs, and keyboard composition. Record what happens on each destination instead of treating source code or a screenshot as an accessibility result.

simple.story: A library gives each book a shelf card with a permanent number. The title on a card can change, and the card can move to another shelf. The number still identifies the same book. A reader needs more than that number: the title must be large enough to read, and the borrow button must be easy to find. Making the print larger should let the card grow or rearrange, rather than hide half its title. Identity, readable content, and usable actions are separate things to check.
simple.meaning: UIKit's diffable list uses stable identifiers while titles and order change. SwiftUI layout must adapt to large text, and accessibility labels must explain controls. Each requires a check beyond simply seeing that the app compiled.

example.before: The UIKit list contains alpha with title Alpha and beta with title Beta.
example.change: Rename alpha to Alpha card, reverse the rows, and select the displayed Alpha card.
example.after: The title updates, beta appears before alpha, and the selection callback still reports alpha. At large text sizes, separately verify the full title is readable and the action remains reachable.

picture.caption: Renaming and moving a row changes content and position while its identifier stays stable.

items.text: The row begins with ID alpha and title Alpha.

items.label: Rename
items.text: Current content changes to Alpha card under the same ID.

items.label: Reverse rows

words.meaning: User-facing words that help explain a control to assistive technology.
A stable testing key, separate from the words a person should hear.
System text sizing that follows the user's preferred reading size.
A description of list sections, item identity, and order used to update a UIKit list.
A SwiftUI adapter that creates, updates, and retires a UIKit view or controller.
Text an input method is still composing and has not yet finalized.

simple.remember: Keep identity stable, update content, and check usability with the actual interaction.
simple.boundary: A shelf card explains row identity. It cannot demonstrate spoken traversal, layout fitting, or input-method composition. A stable ID does not update cell content by itself; reconfiguration is a separate step. Compilation, simulator interaction, and device assistive checks provide different evidence.

sections.title: Decide what a person must be able to do
sections.html:
Accessibility means a person can understand and operate the interface using their chosen input and reading tools. On Android, Compose semantics, font scaling, and TalkBack need checks beyond a screenshot. Apply that habit here. Useful labels, clear grouping, reachable actions, flexible text, and keyboard behavior each need evidence. Finding accessibilityLabel in source is only a starting point. Use the lab README to build, then launch and open Gallery and UIKit. Record the destination and OS version. The generic simulator build shows the app compiles; the following runtime checks establish what a person can actually do.

Choose a compact iPhone and a wide iPad window, then choose a large accessibility text size. Use a long synthetic name to exercise content pressure. Inspect the Gallery card, form controls, presentation actions, and UIKit list. Test portrait and landscape separately. The deployment floor is iOS 17, so every API exercised here belongs in that supported runtime or needs its own availability gate. New behavior in a current SDK does not make older runtime behavior identical.

Write observations as concrete statements: the full title remains readable, the rename action is reachable, the slider announces a useful value, or the popover adapts to a sheet. Avoid writing simply 'accessibility passed'. Sessions 022 and 082 supply the semantic review, 029–031 supply sizing contracts, and 084 supplies the evidence handoff. This workshop adds real source boundaries that the older conceptual labs asked you to create in a scratch target. It leaves actual VoiceOver, Switch Control, hardware keyboard, and visual checks for the learner's runtime record.

sections.title: Let a large title choose a taller layout
sections.html:
A layout proposal is the space a parent offers its child. ViewThatFits(in: .horizontal) tries the card's layout candidates against that space. AdaptiveCard first offers a horizontal title and badge, then a vertical stack. In the horizontal candidate, fixedSize preserves the title's ideal width so a long row fails the fit test rather than shrinking through truncation. At accessibility text sizes, the code skips the horizontal candidate. The vertical version uses semantic body text, permits wrapping, and sets no fixed text height. The goal is a readable title under the actual proposal, not a row forced into one shape.

This resembles choosing a Compose layout from constraints, but it is not a direct equivalent to a measured Android View or a breakpoint-only rule. SwiftUI parents propose dimensions and children choose sizes; a fitting container evaluates candidate descriptions under those proposals. The order matters because the first fitting candidate wins. A title that visually truncates can still technically fit, so inspect the modifiers applied to each candidate. A fixed-size label can be useful for the test candidate and harmful when applied indiscriminately to the fallback.

The UIKit list uses automatic row height and multi-line primary and secondary text. Its default content configuration receives the row values. The dynamic UITextView uses a preferred text-style font, adjusts for content-size-category changes, and disables internal scrolling so its representable can report a growing height. The surrounding SwiftUI container still decides its available space. Extremely long editor content in this intentionally small workbench can pressure that container; a production editor would choose a scroll owner and a content budget rather than promise unlimited growth.

Checkpoint: compare the card at normal and accessibility text sizes, then paste a multi-line synthetic paragraph into the UIKit editor. Confirm text grows within the available area and tab actions remain reachable. Sessions 031 and 033 explain layout and keyboard ownership. This is a bounded demonstration, not a production adaptive layout system or a claim that every window size has been verified.

sections.title: Give spoken controls useful names and values
sections.html:
Semantics describes what an interface element means and what a person can do with it. The slider supplies a label and a percentage value, so a listener gets more than a bare number. The card and badge become one semantic element because the badge adds description and has no separate action. The draft field and task label also have stable accessibility identifiers for future UI automation. Those identifiers are testing keys. Labels are user-facing, spoken content. Keep both roles clear so a person hears meaningful language instead of a machine key. A combined card still needs runtime review to check that the grouping makes sense.

Buttons communicate their action and preserve system roles where possible. Delete and reset use destructive roles, while a confirmation dialog offers cancellation. A disabled validation button still needs an understandable nearby reason, supplied by the draft summary. A custom ButtonStyle must preserve enabled and pressed states instead of decorating a Text with a gesture that discards normal button semantics. Color cannot be the only sign that a control is disabled or that a draft is valid.

Checkpoint: enable VoiceOver on a real destination and navigate the form in order. Confirm that each control exposes its label, value, and action. Increase the slider through assistive interaction, activate a known fixture link, and dismiss the sheet. Inspect whether the combined card reads naturally; combining every row would conceal useful individual actions. The UIKit rename and delete buttons should remain separate controls, even if a screenshot would look tidier with the entire row merged.

VoiceOver behavior in a simulator, a device, and an automated accessibility audit supplies different evidence. A source review can identify likely omissions but cannot certify traversal or speech. Keep failures in your ledger with the exact control and reproduction sequence. Sessions 022, 032, and 082 support follow-up practice; this workshop intentionally avoids claiming that a custom style or an accessibility modifier alone establishes an inclusive product.

sections.title: Change row titles and order without changing IDs
sections.html:
A diffable snapshot describes list membership and order using stable item identifiers. The UIKit tab embeds a real UITableViewController through UIViewControllerRepresentable. Its UITableViewDiffableDataSource uses fixture strings as IDs. The SwiftUI owner can rename Alpha while keeping alpha, or reverse rows without inventing new IDs. A dictionary supplies the current content for each ID. The cell provider captures its controller weakly: the retained data source must not keep a strong reference back to the controller and form a cycle. The code below changes the snapshot and separately asks existing items to refresh their content.

let old = Set(dataSource.snapshot().itemIdentifiers)
var snapshot = NSDiffableDataSourceSnapshot<Int, String>()
snapshot.appendSections([0])
snapshot.appendItems(items.map(\.id))
snapshot.reconfigureItems(items.map(\.id).filter { old.contains($0) })
dataSource.apply(snapshot, animatingDifferences: view.window != nil)

Appending identifiers describes membership and ordering. Reconfiguration explicitly updates content for identifiers that already existed; changing a title alone would not necessarily cause a diff to replace a cell. The intersection avoids asking to reconfigure an item absent from the earlier snapshot. The fixture API expects unique IDs; a production boundary should validate duplicates before constructing its dictionary or applying a snapshot. Session 030 discusses that failure mode and why random per-render IDs defeat reuse.

The controller's selection delegate asks the data source for the selected identifier. It does not infer identity from an array index that might have moved. The representable replaces its selection closure during every update, then applies the newest values. Dismantling clears the callback. Checkpoint: rename Alpha repeatedly, reverse the rows, and select the displayed Alpha. The callback must report alpha and the visible title must update. This is observable UIKit–SwiftUI interoperability, not a static wrapper that happens to render once.

sections.title: Keep the UIKit editor connected to current values
sections.html:
A representable connects a UIKit object to SwiftUI's changing descriptions. GrowingTextView uses UIViewRepresentable. Creation installs the UITextView and its delegate. Update refreshes the coordinator, the helper receiving UIKit callbacks, with the latest representable and its current binding. Then it replaces text only when UIKit and SwiftUI disagree. Delegate callbacks write into that current binding. If update leaves the coordinator holding an old binding, a reused text view can send edits to an obsolete owner while still looking correct. Creation, later updates, and teardown therefore have different jobs.

The update checks markedTextRange before replacing text. An input method may be composing several characters; overwriting that temporary range on each render can destroy the user's editing session. When programmatic replacement is needed, selection is clamped using NSString's UTF-16 length because UIKit's NSRange uses UTF-16 indices. Swift's String.count measures extended grapheme clusters and is not the same indexing system. The character counter shown outside the editor demonstrates the difference in meaning rather than claiming a perfect selection-preservation algorithm.

sizeThatFits accepts SwiftUI's proposed width and asks UITextView for a fitting height. Dismantling removes the delegate. These are modest lifecycle responsibilities: current values in, current events out, measurable size, and explicit teardown. Sessions 010 and 033 connect them to host ownership and text editing. Advanced rich text, selection transformations, undo, input accessories, and scroll coordination remain specialist work.

Checkpoint: type a multi-scalar emoji, edit a selection, and try a composing keyboard. Change an unrelated SwiftUI value while editing. The text should not be reset simply because update runs again. These checks require actual keyboard interaction; the companion's build proves only that the methods and types compile. Capture the smallest failing input and identify whether its range is UTF-16, a Swift string index, or user-perceived characters before implementing a correction.

exercise.brief: Add a fourth UIKit card with a stable ID and a long title. Show which card was renamed, then check row identity, large text, assistive actions, and composing input.
steps: Record the unchanged target's build result. Record launch separately on an available destination.
Add a fixture with ID delta and a long synthetic title to the UIKit tab's local array. Keep delta unique and unchanged after edits.
Show visible rename status naming the affected card. Keep Rename and Delete as separate accessible actions.
Rename cards, reverse the rows, and select one. Check the updated title and returned ID, rather than its array index.
Try large text, assistive navigation, and a composing keyboard. Record the destination, exact input, observed result, and each scenario you could not run.
acceptance: The new fixture has unique stable identity, including after reordering.
The renamed title changes without recreating every identity.
Large text remains readable and actions stay reachable.
A composing input session is not overwritten during unrelated updates.
Source inspection, simulator checks, and real-device assistive checks are labeled separately.
exercise.solution:
Add a FixtureItem with ID delta and a title long enough to wrap. Put it in the UIKit tab's local state. This is a list exercise, so keep the routing allowlist unchanged: adding a card does not authorize a deep-link destination. After Rename or Reverse, its ID must still be delta. The dictionary supplies its latest text, and the next snapshot includes its ID. Later renames reconfigure that existing item; they do not delete it and create a random new identity.

Store rename status in the SwiftUI owner and update it in the same button action that changes the item value. A label such as 'Renamed Alpha card' supplies visible context. If assistive announcement behavior is needed, define when to announce and verify it with VoiceOver; setting a label on a static Text is not an instruction to speak every change. Keep row action buttons independent so the user can choose Rename or Delete.

The input review uses a string containing an emoji and a composed character. Explain why UIKit's selection is clamped against (text as NSString).length, while the visible counter uses text.count. During marked-text composition the representable does not assign its external text into UIKit. That prevents the demonstrated update path from interrupting the input method, although a full editor still needs tests for external replacements and selection semantics.

Your handoff should include the destination, text-size setting, assistive tool, exact action sequence, observed result, and any clipping or unreachable action. If simulator services cannot run, submit the compiled artifact and source reasoning with those runtime rows pending. The original companion supplies mechanisms and worked explanations; it does not pre-fill this acceptance record or establish accessibility certification.

quiz.question: Why reconfigure identifiers that exist in both snapshots?
options: Diffable snapshots always inspect every title
An existing stable identifier can have changed display content
Reconfiguration gives every row a random new identity
quiz.explanation: Membership and identity are separate from display content. Reconfiguration updates cells for existing IDs while preserving identity and ordering semantics.

quiz.question: Why avoid assigning external text while markedTextRange is present?
options: The input method may be composing text that replacement would disrupt
Marked text is always invalid input
Swift String.count uses UTF-16
quiz.explanation: Marked text belongs to an active composition session. UIKit ranges use UTF-16; Swift String.count measures grapheme clusters, so those lengths cannot be substituted.

quiz.question: Which result establishes VoiceOver acceptance?
options: An accessibility identifier exists
A normal-size preview compiled
Recorded traversal and activation on an actual destination with the intended assistive tool
quiz.explanation: Labels, identifiers, and previews support testing. Speech, focus order, reachability, and activation need separate runtime evidence.

workshops.title: Native stores: save a note, then check it after relaunch
workshops.summary: Create and edit notes in two separate stores. Follow Core Data context ownership and SwiftData container, context, and query roles; check saving and relaunch separately.

simple.story: You keep two notebooks, one green and one blue. Writing Tea in the green notebook does not put Tea in the blue one. Reading a note while you still hold a pencil also does not prove you have put the notebook away safely. You finish the entry, close the notebook, and reopen it to check. A helper may write another entry at a different desk, but you ask for a copy of the finished information rather than take the helper's partly edited page.
simple.meaning: The workbench's Core Data and SwiftData editors use independent stores. Each mutation needs a save result. Core Data work belongs to its context, and immutable snapshots carry information to the UI without moving live managed objects across queues.

example.before: The scratch app's two store editors are empty.
example.change: Insert Tea in Core Data and explicitly save it. Close and relaunch the app, then inspect both editors.
example.after: After a successful save and tested relaunch, Core Data should show Tea and SwiftData should remain empty. These are expected observations to verify; the example supplies no executed relaunch result.

picture.caption: A note goes through an explicit Core Data save and relaunch check without appearing in SwiftData.

items.text: Insert a note inside the owning Core Data context.

items.label: Save
items.text: Check the save's success or visible failure.

items.label: Relaunch
items.text: Open the scratch app again and fetch its records.

items.label: Compare stores
items.text: Expect Tea in Core Data and no corresponding SwiftData note.

words.meaning: The stored record's declared shape, including field names, types, and constraints.
The owner that sets up a persistence stack and its contexts.
The working space that owns managed records and performs changes under its access rules.
A separate value containing selected record data, without a live managed object.
An explicit request to persist pending changes, whose result must be checked.
A defined way to open or transform data saved under an older schema.

simple.remember: Name the store owner, keep records within their context, and verify save and relaunch separately.
simple.boundary: The notebooks explain independent stores and completed work. Contexts have queue or isolation rules, not physical desks, and actor isolation does not override those rules. A relaunch check proves only the tested scratch configuration; it does not prove migration, crash recovery, locked-device access, or shared-widget storage.

sections.title: Open two editors with two independent stores
sections.html:
A store holds saved records. CRUD means create, read, update, and delete those records. Room entities and DAOs give you a useful Android starting point; here begin with the actual iOS store and its owner. The Stores tab contains two separate editors. Core Data builds a programmatic NSManagedObjectModel and NSPersistentContainer. SwiftData uses an @Model type and ModelContainer. Inserting a note into Core Data does not insert it into SwiftData. Keeping them independent lets you inspect each construction and CRUD path. This workshop supplies no migration or synchronization between the two.

Build and launch using the lab README, then open Stores. Initially both editors should be empty because the lab does not auto-seed completed work. Use Insert and save explicitly. Record insertion, rename, and deletion in each editor. A relaunch after an explicit save is the next durability checkpoint; a row remaining visible while the process is alive proves only memory behavior. Use synthetic titles. The stores are confined to the scratch app's sandbox, with no company schema or account data.

The Core Data SQLite file lives under Application Support in the SwiftUIWorkbench directory. The SwiftData container uses its default sandbox storage location. Previews select memory-only storage. Startup errors are visible and do not trigger automatic destructive recovery. No code deletes an old store to hide a model mismatch. Session 083 supplies a first SwiftData path, while sessions 019, 020, and 053 cover production ownership, cache boundaries, and migration questions. This lab fills the earlier gap between a conceptual cache discussion and a constructed native store.

sections.title: Make and change records only in their owning context
sections.html:
A schema names the fields a saved record must contain. CoreNote's Core Data schema has three required attributes: UUID identity, String title, and Date creation time. NSManagedObject is the live, context-owned record. The programmatic NSManagedObjectModel declares its attribute types and a uniqueness constraint for identity. There is no xcdatamodeld resource to compile, but the declaration still creates a persisted schema. Once data has been saved, renaming a field or changing its type raises compatibility questions. Writing the model in code does not remove versioning or migration responsibilities.

The persistent container owns the coordinator and contexts. Its view context is used from the store's main-actor methods. Insert creates an object in that context, assigns all required attributes, and calls save. Rename fetches by UUID, updates the title, and saves. Delete fetches the current object by identity, marks it for deletion, and saves. Fetch sorts by creation date and converts live managed objects to immutable CoreNoteSnapshot values for the SwiftUI interface. The interface never carries a managed object into an unrelated queue.

If a view-context save fails, the example rolls back that context and exposes the failure. This is a chosen tutorial policy for a tiny context with no multi-screen draft changes. A production editor may need to preserve user edits, identify the failing transaction, and present retry. Rolling back a shared context indiscriminately can discard other pending changes. Similarly, a property-trump merge policy is a conflict choice, not an explanation that no conflicts can happen.

Checkpoint: insert two distinct titles, rename one repeatedly, and delete the other. Observe stable UUID identity while text changes. The API uses a UUID predicate rather than an index or table position. Core Data performs work under its context rules even when a caller is actor-isolated. An actor protecting a repository does not grant permission to access arbitrary context-bound objects on its executor. Session 053 makes that boundary explicit; the lab demonstrates it with value snapshots.

sections.title: Save on a background context and return plain values
sections.html:
A background context owns a separate working set of Core Data objects on its own queue. The Background context insert button asks the persistent container to create one. Its perform closure creates and saves a synthetic note under that queue's rules. The live managed object stays inside the closure. When the asynchronous call finishes, the caller resumes on the main actor, processes pending view-context changes, and refreshes immutable snapshots for the screen. automaticallyMergesChangesFromParent also lets the view context accept relevant container saves. Saving, merging, and fetching UI values are related steps with separate outcomes.

let context = container.newBackgroundContext()
try await context.perform {
    let object = NSEntityDescription.insertNewObject(
        forEntityName: "CoreNote", into: context)
    object.setValue(UUID(), forKey: "id")
    object.setValue("Background fixture", forKey: "title")
    object.setValue(Date(), forKey: "createdAt")
    try context.save()
}
// Refresh UI snapshots on the main actor after this succeeds.

This is target-dependent Core Data code. The inserted object belongs to the background context for its whole lifetime. Passing its UUID or a permanent object ID is possible in a larger design; passing the live object to another context is not. Saving and merging are distinct operations: saving makes the transaction available to the persistent store, and merging reconciles another context's registered objects. The visible refresh is an explicit fetch, so seeing the new row alone does not prove that every possible existing-object merge scenario passed.

Checkpoint: add a background fixture and verify its title appears, then relaunch and verify the saved record still exists. The button is disabled while its operation is running to keep this UI exercise bounded. This sample inserts in the background; it does not implement background update conflict testing, cancellation of a transaction in progress, multi-process coordination, or an account epoch. Add those as separate scenarios before proposing a production design. Main-actor UI ownership, Core Data queue confinement, and durable store ownership remain three related but distinct responsibilities.

sections.title: Give SwiftData a model, container, and context
sections.html:
A SwiftData model declares a kind of stored record. @Model adds persistence support to PracticeNote, whose UUID is marked unique. The app then creates a ModelContainer to own the store and installs it above the interface with modelContainer. The editor gets its working context through modelContext. @Query supplies notes sorted by creation time for presentation. Keep these roles distinct: the model declares the schema, the container owns setup and lifetime, the context performs operations, and the query supplies results. Creating a model instance alone does not open an on-disk store.

Insert explicitly calls context.insert and then context.save. Rename changes a model property and saves; Delete calls context.delete and saves. The editor records successful saves and rolls back failures. SwiftData can autosave in supported UI contexts, but this lab uses explicit saves so the moment of intended durability is visible. It does not treat an updated query result as proof that the disk write succeeded.

The Query reads managed model instances within the UI context boundary. Do not send those references into Task.detached just because the declaration resembles an ordinary class. A larger background pipeline can use ModelActor or another reviewed isolation design and exchange identifiers or Sendable values. Observation of a property, persistence of a record, and permission to access that record from another executor are different contracts. Session 076 introduces model ownership; 083 and 053 extend it to stores.

Checkpoint: switch between the two segmented editors and confirm their records remain independent. Insert a SwiftData note, rename it, relaunch, and verify the title; delete it, relaunch again, and verify absence. This project requires iOS 17 for SwiftData, Observation integration, and the widget's interactive button. Testing with a recent simulator SDK proves compilation for its deployment settings, not that every earliest-supported OS behavior was executed.

sections.title: Record the storage promises you still need to test
sections.html:
A production storage contract states whose data is stored, who may change it, and how failures are handled. This scratch app uses synthetic notes. It has no real users, account IDs, replication, encryption feature, old-schema migration fixture, or shared extension access. A UUID identifies a note; it does not authorize a user. A uniqueness constraint does not separate accounts. Production work needs explicit rules for logout, account replacement, late background writes, unavailable protected data, backup, and retention. Session 053 and the production data lab discuss those responsibilities. Keep them as separate requirements rather than assuming the two CRUD editors satisfy them.

Model changes deserve old-store fixtures and upgrade evidence. Before modifying a persisted attribute, save an example with the old schema and preserve it outside the learner's current scratch run. Define whether a compatible migration is lightweight, requires a transformation, or needs a new versioned schema plan. Never call a fresh installation test a successful migration test. Deleting and reinstalling the scratch app is an explicit local reset that discards its stores, not a recovery procedure for users.

Core Data's sibling contexts do not share a single mutable object graph, and SwiftData is not an automatic replacement for every Core Data capability. Choose one technology from requirements, isolation, testability, migration needs, and supported platforms. The two editors make the differences inspectable without proposing that the company client migrate. A successful compile and visible CRUD sequence are modest evidence; they do not cover disk-full errors, concurrent updates, corruption, protected-data locking, or data recovery.

Checkpoint: finish a small evidence ledger containing store construction, explicit save, value snapshot ownership, background save result, query update, relaunch result, and failure-policy review. Mark a relaunch or hardware storage test pending when it was not run. Session 084's handoff should state the exact verified boundary and identify specialist work. Your exercise below adds a read transformation without adding a third source of truth or allowing live managed references to cross queues.

exercise.brief: Filter the displayed titles in both editors. Give Core Data's background insert a title input, while keeping saved records, context access, and save results intact.
steps: Compile and launch when a destination is available. In each store, save notes named Tea and Toast; the two stores must remain independent.

Add a local search string. Derive displayed Core Data snapshots from the full current array; do not replace that array with filtered state. Tea should show one row and clearing the filter should restore both.
Filter SwiftData query results for display, or explain a bounded predicate-based Query with its supported input rules. Filtering must not delete notes.
Pass an immutable title String to addInBackground. Validate it before starting, then assign it only inside context.perform.
Record create, rename, delete, and relaunch results separately. Explain why the background closure returns no live managed object to the UI.
acceptance: Clearing the filter restores existing saved records without reinsertion.
Background insertion returns no live managed object to the UI.
Explicit save success and save failure remain visible.
SwiftData and Core Data are described as separate stores.
Migration, shared-widget storage, and device locking are not claimed verified.
exercise.solution:
Keep a local @State filter in the Core Data editor. Compute displayed snapshots by checking each current title with localizedCaseInsensitiveContains. With Tea and Toast saved, filter Tea shows one row; clearing it shows both. Do not assign the filtered array back into the store. This changes presentation without removing records or storing a second copy of the data. The small synthetic set is easy to inspect. A larger production store needs suitable query filtering, fetch limits, and measured cost.

Change the background method to accept title: String, validate the bounded nonempty input before starting, and capture that immutable value inside the context's perform closure. Create, assign, and save the NSManagedObject entirely in that closure. After it succeeds, refresh main-actor snapshots. An error should remain visible rather than being swallowed by try?. The returned value can be a UUID or a Sendable snapshot if needed, never the background managed object itself.

For SwiftData, a computed filter over the existing Query results changes display without deleting model instances. If you implement an actual predicate-based Query instead, describe how the filter becomes the query input and verify its supported predicate expressions. Saving remains explicit in all mutation actions. The production tradeoff is query cost and data volume, not whether one API has fewer lines.

Record insertion, filtered visibility, rename, clear-filter recovery, background save, deletion, and relaunch for each technology. Relaunch evidence establishes this scratch app's persistence for the tested configuration; it does not establish migration from an old schema or durability shared with a widget. The widget in this project uses independent synthetic data and never opens either store. Keep unexecuted storage-failure and hardware checks pending in the handoff.

quiz.question: What may safely leave the background Core Data operation in this design?
options: Its live NSManagedObject
Its context for arbitrary UI access
A UUID or immutable Sendable snapshot
quiz.explanation: Context confinement continues to apply. Values and suitable identities can cross the boundary; another context must resolve its own managed object.

quiz.question: A new row appeared after refresh. What still needs separate evidence?
options: Existing-object merge behavior and relaunch durability
Whether the String type exists
Whether both editors use one shared store
quiz.explanation: The UI refresh performs a fetch. Its visible result does not independently prove every merge scenario, and process-alive visibility is not a relaunch test.

quiz.question: Why save SwiftData explicitly after mutation here?
options: Query is itself a disk transaction
The practice makes intended durability and failures observable
ModelContainer automatically synchronizes Core Data notes
quiz.explanation: Explicit saves expose the intended boundary and its errors. Query updates and container construction do not establish successful disk writes or cross-store synchronization.

workshops.title: Platform adapters: validate inputs and retire old work
workshops.summary: Use explicit controls for local notifications, links, photos, location, camera, and local web content. Trace each effect's owner and cleanup, and keep authentication and widget limits visible.

simple.story: A reception desk accepts delivery slips with one exact format. A slip names the desk, the shelf, and one known parcel number. The clerk checks every part before sending anyone to a shelf. Extra instructions scribbled at the bottom are not accepted, even when the parcel number looks right. Rejecting a slip means staying where you are. An accepted slip only chooses a shelf in this small practice room. It does not prove who wrote the slip or give permission to enter other rooms.
simple.meaning: WorkbenchLink accepts only the declared fixture URL vocabulary. The same parser serves app links and notification routing. Each other platform effect also needs an explicit owner, current-attempt checks, and cleanup; parser success does not provide authentication.

example.before: Gallery has its current path, and alpha is an allowed fixture ID.
example.change: Give the parser workbench://gallery/item/alpha?debug=1 instead of the exact workbench://gallery/item/alpha URL.
example.after: The query-bearing URL is rejected, so it must not change navigation. In the exercise, the rejection counter increases by one without storing the raw URL. The exact URL remains an accepted alpha route.

picture.caption: A link with an extra query is refused before it can change the router.

items.label: Incoming URL
items.text: The input names alpha but also contains ?debug=1.

items.label: Exact parser
items.text: The parser requires the literal bounded route with no query.

items.label: Keep current path
items.text: Only the proposed generic rejection count changes.

words.meaning: An owned wrapper that translates system APIs into the app's chosen operations and outcomes.
An object a framework calls when an event or result needs handling.
A changing attempt marker used to reject callbacks from earlier work.
Here, a random marker identifying the currently installed local web document.
The system's permission decision for an app capability, separate from a successful operation.
A running program boundary; the widget does not share the app's in-memory owners.

simple.remember: Accept only known input, and let only the current owner accept a platform result.
simple.boundary: The reception desk explains a narrow parser, not caller identity or system delivery. Cancellation can retire acceptance while photo decoding or a permission dialog continues. Local notifications do not prove APNs delivery. The unconfigured auth adapter and independent widget provide no validated login or shared-store durability.

sections.title: Give each system effect a lasting owner
sections.html:
An adapter is an app-owned wrapper around a system operation. It turns framework calls and callbacks into the app's chosen outcomes. Android permission launchers, activity results, and retained service owners give useful examples, but iOS delegates and lifetimes have different rules. Open Platform in the compiled scratch app. Each permission or device operation begins with a named button. AppServices retains the adapters so they survive beyond a tap closure and can reject retired callbacks. Startup requests no runtime permission, opens no identity provider, and loads no remote resource. Trace the owner before trying the effect.

Read the lab's exact verification record before using the controls. The generic simulator build covers SwiftUI, UIKit, WebKit, persistence, device-service declarations, and the embedded widget product. The route checks run the pure Foundation parser on the host. These results do not establish a location fix, camera capture, Photos picker completion, notification delivery, or widget interaction. Simulator services were unavailable during authoring. Hardware camera and authorization behavior remain device checks; camera unavailability on a simulator is a supported outcome.

Use only synthetic practice media and titles. Picked images remain in memory and are not uploaded or saved to Photos. Location coordinates are discarded after reporting whether a fix was available and whether accuracy was reduced. The lab does not request background location, broad photo-library authorization, microphone access, push-notification registration, universal-link association, or App Groups. Sessions 050–056 supply those wider design boundaries. This companion implements a modest explicit effect surface, not a production privacy or security certification.

sections.title: Validate a route before changing navigation
sections.html:
A local notification is scheduled by this app on the device; it is different from a remote APNs push. The notification adapter is a retained NSObject. Before the interface is used, it installs itself as the notification center's weak delegate, the object called for notification events. Request permission asks for alert and sound authorization. Schedule checks current settings and does not silently prompt when permission is absent. One named request schedules a synthetic notification for five seconds with an Alpha route in userInfo. Clear removes only that request and its delivered notification. Scheduling still needs separate runtime delivery and response checks.

The application registers the workbench custom URL scheme in its plist and handles incoming URLs through onOpenURL. Notification responses call the same router. The app-owned router already exists independently of Gallery, so a cold launch can retain its selected tab and path before the screen appears. A warm route replaces the known gallery path. Custom schemes are not authenticated callers or universal-link domain associations; parser success grants access only to the harmless fixture vocabulary.

WorkbenchLink rejects unexpected schemes, hosts, credentials, ports, query strings, fragments, extra path components, encoded aliases, and unknown IDs. Its input length is bounded. It uses the percent-encoded path so an encoded slash or encoded spelling cannot bypass the literal vocabulary. The host check script exercises accepted and rejected fixtures against the same parser compiled into the app. A hostile link does not become a network URL or database predicate.

Checkpoint: use the README's simulator openurl command with Alpha while the app is running, then terminate the app and repeat for Beta. Record the selected tab and detail. Schedule the local notification, move to the Home screen, tap its alert, and repeat with the app terminated. These are separate runtime scenarios; scheduling success alone is not evidence of a displayed alert or cold response. Sessions 051 and 079 explain route validation and navigation, while 050 explains delivery and background limits.

sections.title: Install a local web document and remove its callbacks
sections.html:
A web view displays a document in a WebKit process. The Install web view toggle creates a real WKWebView with a non-persistent data store, so this exercise uses a temporary web storage owner. It loads an HTML string bundled in source, without a remote base URL or remote resources. A restrictive content-security policy limits the page. The navigation delegate accepts only the local about:blank main document and rejects other destinations and popups. The bridge exposes no general JavaScript evaluator. This local document policy belongs to this exercise; a remote page would need a reviewed HTTPS origin and document policy.

The user-content controller retains a weak-forwarding script handler. A document-end user script supplies one function that posts a two-field acknowledgment message. The coordinator checks the message name, current web view, main frame, empty local security-origin host, current document URL, exact action, and current random nonce. Replacing the local document rotates that nonce and installs a new user script, so a previous document's callback cannot become the current acknowledgment. A nonce here is a document-lifetime marker, not a general authorization secret or proof that arbitrary web content is trusted.

The cookie buttons install a synthetic cookie for workbench.invalid or remove cookies from this ephemeral store. They wait for cookie-store completion and check current document/command identity before updating status. No navigation follows cookie installation, and no cookie value is printed as a credential. Toggling the web view off stops loading, removes handlers and scripts, clears delegates, and retires the coordinator's active document identity. Reinstalling uses a new ephemeral store and does not replay an old cookie command.

Checkpoint: acknowledge the current document, replace it, acknowledge again, install and clear the fixture cookie, and remove the web view. Inspect teardown in the source. Runtime WebKit process behavior and actual stale-message timing still require separate interaction evidence. Session 054 supplies the broader origin, cookie, and authentication trust model; this lab gives you actual install and removal code to reason about rather than merely naming WKWebView.

sections.title: Retain an auth attempt without calling it a login
sections.html:
An authentication session is the system browser flow an app can use for a provider interaction. SystemAuthAdapter keeps an optional ASWebAuthenticationSession and receives a presentation window belonging to the caller's scene. start accepts an HTTPS URL and callback scheme, retains the session before starting it, and installs its presentation context provider. A generation ticket marks the current attempt. Completion enters the main actor and clears the session and window only if that ticket is still current. Cancel advances the generation and releases the retained session. These steps manage lifetime; they do not validate a provider response or establish a login.

The actual interface supplies a cleanup button and explains that no provider is configured. It never calls start automatically or presents a provider start button. The adapter is reviewable implementation scaffolding: a future integration must define its provider allowlist, callback validation, OAuth state, PKCE, credential ownership, and failure policy before trusting a callback. The status deliberately says a callback still requires validation rather than claiming authentication succeeded merely because the system returned a URL.

An ephemeral browser preference requests a session mode; it is not a blanket guarantee about every provider's storage or a method for sharing WKWebView cookies. The system authentication surface and an app-created web view are distinct owners. A weak window reference avoids retaining a dismissed scene, while the active session remains strongly retained until its terminal outcome. The caller must start with a live window belonging to its intended scene. A single global 'first window' lookup would hide multi-window ownership.

Checkpoint: inspect start, cancel, presentationAnchor, and completion ordering, then use Cancel to observe cleanup status without starting any provider. Do not manufacture a real login test with an invented callback URL. Sessions 025 and 054 identify the trust and credential responsibilities; 034 and 081 explain scene and task lifetimes. The source compiles as an adapter, but real provider invocation and protocol validation remain unexecuted and unimplemented respectively.

sections.title: Keep only the current photo or permission result
sections.html:
A photo selection starts a load that may finish after the person chooses something else. PhotosPicker opens on an explicit tap without requesting broad library authorization. PhotoSelection owns the asynchronous load. Its Transferable type describes how to import image Data. It rejects inputs over 12 MiB after transfer, then downsamples the image off the main actor. That late size check allows a large Data buffer to exist first; it is not a streaming memory bound. Detached thumbnail decoding may continue after cancellation. Cancellation and generation checks keep that old output from becoming the current thumbnail.

Select A and then B before A finishes. A's completion must not replace B. Clear cancels the retained task, increments the generation, and removes the thumbnail. A canceled picker that does not change selection may emit no new item; that is why there is also an explicit clear/cancel action. The sample does not represent cancellation as a fictitious new photo or ask for library permission just to learn whether the picker was dismissed.

LocationAdapter owns a fresh CLLocationManager per request. It handles denied, restricted, unavailable, and successful-fix outcomes, requests authorization only on the button action, and requests a single fix when allowed. Delegate trampolines enter the main actor, compare manager identity, and discard retired callbacks. Cancel stops updates, removes the delegate, and releases the manager. A timeout is not guaranteed by the framework, so the explicit cancel action matters. Reduced accuracy is reported without silently requesting temporary full accuracy.

CameraAdapter checks hardware availability and authorization, waits for permission if required, and compares a generation ticket before presenting a system still-camera controller. Cancellation during the permission wait prevents late presentation. The controller's retained coordinator handles capture and user cancellation; captured pixels stay in memory. Leaving Platform or backgrounding the scene retires photo, camera, location, and authentication work. Checkpoint: cancel a pending load, cancel a permission wait, deny access, and revisit the screen. Session 055's capability matrix and 081's commit guards guide the observations; successful permissions alone do not prove session ownership.

sections.title: Treat the widget as a separate running program
sections.html:
A widget extension is a separate product running outside the app's process. This project embeds a minimal WidgetKit extension with a placeholder, snapshot, and synthetic timeline. A timeline supplies entries for the system to display. Small and medium layouts show Alpha and an AppIntent button. The intent returns a dialog saying that no data was saved. The timeline requests a later refresh; the system does not promise the exact requested execution time. Its local fixture URL is understood by the containing app's parser. Compile, installation, displayed entries, and intent execution need separate evidence.

No App Group entitlement is present, neither store is shared, and the extension does not read app-owned services. Its acknowledgment is not durable interprocess mutation. An actor or MainActor inside the extension would still be local to that process. Before adding real shared state, define an actual transactional store or command protocol, ownership validation, replay policy, and signed capability configuration. A widget reload request would not itself establish that a write was durable or a new timeline was rendered.

Checkpoint: after installing and launching the app on a functioning simulator, add Synthetic workbench from the widget gallery, inspect both supported sizes, open its fixture URL, and exercise the intent. Treat these as pending until performed. The compiler builds and embeds the extension here, but authoring did not install a widget or execute its intent. Session 056 supplies extension process, snapshot privacy, refresh, and interprocess boundaries. A worked companion can make those distinctions tangible without claiming production widget support or signed distribution.

exercise.brief: Count rejected links without keeping their text. Make a results table for routing, stale photos, denied or cancelled services, web-view cleanup, and the separate widget process.
steps: Run the host route checks, then compile the app and embedded extension. Record those results separately.
Add a rejected-link counter in the parser-failure branch. An extra-query alpha URL should add one rejection without navigating; keep the allowed routes unchanged and retain no raw URL.
When simulator services work, use the README's openurl commands to check routing while the app is running and after termination.
Select photo A, then B before A finishes; clear during a load. Record current-generation results separately from dismissing the picker without changing selection.
On suitable hardware, review location and camera denial and cancellation. Also check local web install/removal and inspect the unconfigured auth adapter without starting a provider.
Record widget compilation, installation, displayed content, and intent execution in separate rows. Mark unrun rows pending and explain that neither store is shared.
acceptance: Rejected input cannot navigate or expose raw untrusted URLs in status text.
Only current photo/permission generations commit output.
Web scripts and message handlers are removed during teardown.
No provider is invoked, no network auto-call is added, and no permission is requested on appearance.
The ledger explicitly leaves unexecuted hardware/provider/widget scenarios pending and never claims App Group durability.
exercise.solution:
In the router's failed-parser branch, increment a local rejection count and show a generic status. One input such as workbench://gallery/item/alpha?debug=1 should add one rejection and leave navigation unchanged. Keep the parser's requirements intact: recognized scheme, exact host, literal bounded path, no credentials, port, query, or fragment, and a known fixture ID. Retain no raw URL; rejected future inputs may still contain private text. Use the existing host checks against the app's actual parser source, rather than writing a second teaching parser.

The photo ledger contains A selected, B selected before A completed, clear during load, picker dismissed without selection change, oversize import, and unreadable-image failure. For each row identify the generation at commit and whether the actual device sequence was executed. Cancellation retires acceptance immediately even if system work continues. The permission ledger similarly distinguishes authorization status, service availability, user cancellation, late callback, and scene retirement.

The WebKit review traces configuration to weak handler, current document nonce, narrow message validation, asynchronous cookie completion, and dismantle removal. Authentication review traces strong session retention and current-attempt cleanup while keeping start unused. A real provider would require protocol validation outside this scaffold. Do not substitute 'callback received' for a validated login.

The widget ledger records compile/embed evidence, a pending installed snapshot check, a pending intent interaction check, and an absent shared store. A proposed durable design must supply a real interprocess transaction and signed App Group configuration before describing shared mutation as implemented. Your handoff names the exact build command, host test result, destination limitations, and the practical residual work. The companion provides source and worked reasoning; completing this ledger still requires your own observations.

quiz.question: Why retain an ASWebAuthenticationSession and check its attempt ticket?
options: Retention proves the callback is authenticated
The session must survive presentation, and obsolete completion must not update the current attempt
WKWebView automatically supplies OAuth state
quiz.explanation: Lifetime and current-attempt acceptance are separate from provider trust. State/PKCE and callback validation remain required and are not implemented by this scaffold.

quiz.question: What prevents photo A from replacing photo B after a slow transfer?
options: The cancellation check and current-generation comparison before commit
PhotosPicker always completes requests in selection order
The photo filename is a durable account identifier
quiz.explanation: System work can finish late or ignore cancellation for a period. Only the current generation is allowed to commit to UI state.

quiz.question: What does the widget's synthetic intent establish?
options: App Group transactional durability
Synchronization with both app databases
A compiled intent that returns a synthetic dialog without saving shared state
quiz.explanation: The extension has independent fixtures and no shared entitlement or store. Compilation and a synthetic dialog are deliberately smaller claims than interprocess durable mutation.
